doc.title: Clay Jenkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 18, 2016

title: Teaching blues phrasing and 'worried notes'
summary: They discuss playing blues in every key, answering phrases, and nuance in the blue notes.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: The other interesting thing for a horn player if you go to blues jam sessions, you’d better be ready to play in some tougher keys.

That’s right. Guitars. You better be. I make my students, you know we play the blues in every key every day, just on your own with a metronome. Be able to play what you’re hearing and make — and it’s also, you know — when I was younger I would play — I was okay, but I didn’t make that statement like what we call kind of the A-A-B or the consequent phrase. Like so many blues songs, “I left my baby and don’t know what to do” with a period there. And then for a chance for the listener to absorb it. And the next four bars on the four chord, the same thing. We that aren’t so steeped in the blues, we need to be taught that. And so I really bug my students about that. Because they’ll play the blues and they’re playing all this vocabulary and I’m like, “I’ve got to hear that thing.”
I have a neat thing with Clark Terry and Joe Williams talking about THE blue notes.

Yeah. Those worried notes. Oh yeah. Well that’s all in the gesture too. And the nuance. Yeah. And those guys and the Delta guys, they didn’t know the third and the flatted third and all that. So it was nuanced. It was worrying that stuff. That’s the way a friend of mine described it. Worrying the third, worrying the fifth. Yeah. It’s really important.
